title: Meta Descriptions That Get Clicks: Length, Examples, Mistakes
excerpt: How to write a meta description that earns the click: realistic length guidance, why Google rewrites snippets, examples by page type, and fixes at scale.
meta_title: Meta Description Guide: Length, Examples, Mistakes
meta_description: Write a meta description that earns clicks: ideal length, why Google shows other text, real examples by page type, and how to fix missing or duplicates.

content_html:
Search for your own business and look closely at the two lines of grey text under your result. On a lot of small sites, that text is a cookie notice, a footer address, or the first line of a navigation menu. On others, every page shows the exact same sentence.

That text is the snippet, and the main thing you control in it is the meta description. It will not move you up the rankings, but it can be the deciding factor in whether someone clicks your result or the one below it.

This guide covers what a meta description actually does, how long it should be, why Google sometimes ignores yours, a simple formula for writing one, examples for different page types, and how to fix missing or duplicate descriptions across a whole site. It is one item in a wider pre-publish on-page SEO checklist, and it is worth getting right on every page that matters.

What a meta description is (and what it is not)

A meta description is an HTML tag in the <head> of a page. Visitors never see it on the page itself. It looks like this:

<meta name="description" content="Custom birthday and wedding cakes baked to order in Leeds. Gluten-free options, free local delivery, order online up to 48 hours ahead.">

Google may use that text as the snippet under your title in search results. The meta description is a sales pitch for the click, not a ranking signal. Google has said directly that it does not use the description meta tag for ranking, even though it sometimes shows it as the snippet.

So the job is simple: convince the right searcher that this page has what they want. The title and the description work as a pair, so write them together. If you have not tightened up your titles yet, start with writing title tags that get clicked, then write the description to add what the title could not fit.

What to do:

  • Treat the description as ad copy for one specific page, not a summary of your whole business.
  • Do not stuff it with keywords hoping to rank. It will not help rankings and it makes the snippet less readable.
  • Read your title and description out loud together. If they repeat each other word for word, rewrite the description.

Meta description length: how long should it be?

There is no official character limit. Google's snippet documentation says there is no limit on how long a meta description can be, but the snippet is truncated as needed, typically to fit the device width.

In practice, a range of about 70 to 155 characters works well. Under 70 characters you are usually leaving useful space empty and saying too little. Over about 155, the end of your text is likely to be cut off with an ellipsis on many screens. Because truncation depends on display width, not an exact character count, put the most important information in the first sentence.

LengthWhat usually happensWhat to do
MissingGoogle builds a snippet from page text, which may be a menu, notice, or random paragraphWrite one for every important page
Under 70 charactersShows in full but often says too little to win the clickAdd a specific detail: price, location, format, or benefit
About 70 to 155 charactersUsually shows in full on most devicesAim here, with the key point first
Over 155 charactersOften truncated mid-sentenceCut filler or move the essential part to the start

Say you sell handmade leather wallets. "Handmade wallets." is 17 characters and tells the searcher almost nothing. "Handmade full-grain leather wallets, stitched by hand in small batches. Free UK delivery and a 2-year guarantee on every wallet." is around 130 characters and answers the questions a buyer actually has.

Why Google sometimes shows different text

Writing a great description does not guarantee Google will show it. According to Google, snippets are created primarily from the page content, and the meta description is used when it describes the page better than other parts of the content. The snippet is also chosen per search, so the same page can show different text for different queries.

Take a hypothetical bakery page about custom cakes. Its description talks about birthday and wedding cakes. Someone searches for "gluten free celebration cake". Google may skip the description and show the paragraph on the page that mentions gluten-free options, because that matches the search better.

That is not a failure. Google is more likely to replace your description when it is vague, stuffed with keywords, duplicated across many pages, or out of date. Common triggers:

  • A list of keywords instead of a sentence ("cakes, birthday cakes, wedding cakes, Leeds cakes").
  • The same description used on dozens of pages.
  • A description that does not match the page, for example one that still mentions a sale that ended months ago.
  • A description so short that it says nothing a searcher could use.

Google also supports snippet controls such as the nosnippet and max-snippet robots rules and the data-nosnippet attribute. These limit or block snippets. They do not force Google to use your meta description, so most small sites do not need them.

A simple formula for writing a meta description

You do not need to be a copywriter. Most good descriptions answer three questions in one or two sentences:

  1. What is on this page? Match what the searcher is looking for, using the words they would use.
  2. What makes it worth clicking? One specific detail: price range, location, number of options, turnaround time, a free tool, or who it is for.
  3. What can they do next? Book, compare, download, order, or learn, stated plainly.

A few writing rules make a big difference:

  • Use the page's main topic or keyword naturally, once. It confirms to the searcher that they are in the right place.
  • Be specific. "Fast delivery" is forgettable. "Delivered in 2 working days" is useful, as long as it is true.
  • Write in an active voice and talk to the reader.
  • Never promise anything the page does not deliver. A click that bounces straight back helps no one.

Meta description examples by page type

All the businesses below are hypothetical. Use them as patterns, not as copy to paste.

Home page

Weak: "Welcome to Smith Plumbing. We are a plumbing company. Call us today!"

Better: "Family-run plumbers covering Bristol and Bath. Boiler repairs, leaks and bathroom installs, with upfront fixed prices and same-day callouts on weekdays."

The better version names the area, the main services, and two reasons to choose this business.

Product page

Weak: "Buy now! Best prices on the best products. Shop our amazing range today."

Better: "Waterproof 30L hiking backpack with a padded laptop sleeve and rain cover. Weighs 1.1 kg. Free returns within 30 days."

Google's snippet guidance points out that a good description can bring together key facts scattered across a product page, such as price or manufacturer. Concrete details like size, weight, or materials are exactly what a shopper scans for. Prices and ratings can also appear in results through markup, which is covered in our guide to adding structured data to your pages.

Blog post

Weak: "In this post we talk about composting and everything you need to know about it."

Better: "Start a compost bin in a small garden: what to add, what to leave out, and how to fix a smelly or slow heap in a few weeks."

The better version tells the reader exactly which problems the post solves.

Local service page

Weak: "Dog grooming services. Contact us for more information."

Better: "Dog grooming in Northampton for all breeds: bath, cut and nail trim from £35. Online booking with evening and Saturday slots available."

Location, price, and availability are the three things a local searcher compares, so lead with them.

Common meta description mistakes

Most problems fall into a handful of patterns. Check your key pages for each:

  • Missing descriptions. Common on blog archives, tag pages, and pages created years ago before anyone thought about SEO.
  • Duplicates. Themes and plugins often reuse the site tagline on every page. Google's documentation is clear that identical or similar descriptions on every page are not helpful. Duplicate descriptions often travel with duplicate titles, so it is worth reading about what duplicate content actually hurts while you fix them.
  • Template leftovers. Default text like "Just another WordPress site" or a placeholder from a page builder.
  • Keyword lists. Comma-separated terms instead of a sentence.
  • Stale details. Old prices, last year's date, discontinued products, or an offer that has ended.
  • Out-of-range length. A five-word description or a 300-character paragraph.

How to fix missing or duplicate meta descriptions at scale

Rewriting descriptions one page at a time is fine for a 10-page site. For anything bigger, you need a list first and a priority order second.

1. Get a complete list

Crawl the site so you see every page, not just the ones you remember. A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO flags pages with missing or duplicate meta descriptions, and ones outside 70 to 155 characters, and you can export the results to CSV to work through in a spreadsheet.

2. Prioritize by impressions

Not every page deserves the same effort. In Search Console, the Performance report shows impressions, clicks, and click-through rate for each page. Start with your home page and the pages that get the most impressions. A page with many impressions and a low click-through rate is the best candidate for a rewrite, because the snippet is clearly being seen.

3. Use templates for large, similar page sets

For shops or directories with hundreds of similar pages, hand-writing every description is not realistic. Google's documentation supports generating descriptions programmatically from page data, as long as the result is readable and specific to each page. A hypothetical product template might look like this:

[Product name] in [colour], [one key spec]. [Price]. Free returns within 30 days.

Make sure every field is filled for every page. A template that outputs "in , . ." when data is missing is worse than no description at all.

4. Re-check after Google recrawls

Changes only show once Google has recrawled the page, which can take days or weeks. Compare click-through rate for the edited pages over the same length of time before and after the change, and keep in mind that seasonality and ranking changes also affect it.

The bottom line

A meta description is not a ranking factor, but it shapes the first impression of your page in search results. Write a unique, specific description of roughly 70 to 155 characters for every important page, lead with the key point, and keep it true to what is on the page.

Google will sometimes show other text instead, and that is normal. What you can control is giving it a description good enough to use, and making sure no important page is missing one or sharing one with a dozen others.

Your next step: crawl your site, export every page with a missing or duplicate meta description, and rewrite the ten with the most impressions in Search Console this week.

faqs.question: Do meta descriptions affect SEO rankings?
faqs.answer: No. Google has said it does not use the meta description for ranking. It can still affect how many people click your result, which is why it is worth writing well.

faqs.question: Why is Google not showing my meta description?
faqs.answer: Google picks the snippet for each search and primarily uses page content. If your description is vague, duplicated, outdated, or does not match what the person searched for, Google may show a more relevant passage from the page instead.

faqs.question: How many characters should a meta description be?
faqs.answer: Google sets no official limit, but snippets are truncated to fit the screen. Around 70 to 155 characters is a practical target, with the most important information in the first sentence.

faqs.question: Is it bad to have the same meta description on every page?
faqs.answer: It is not a penalty, but it wastes the snippet. Google's documentation says identical or similar descriptions are not helpful, and Google is more likely to ignore them and generate its own text.

faqs.question: Should every page have a meta description?
faqs.answer: Every page you want people to find in search should have one, starting with your home page and most visited pages. For very large sites, generating descriptions from page data is acceptable if the result is readable and specific.
